utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. I would like to know whether you are hearing me in a language that you can understand. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic, I put the same question to you. Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We can have the case summoned now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Brdjanin and Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this morning, Joanna Korner; hiding behind me, Andrew Cayley; and Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, along with Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Ackerman. Maitre de Roux, appearances for General Talic? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Xavier de Roux, Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic and Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you as well. Yes, Ms. Korner, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst we are in open session, and before we continue with the witness, can I mention something in relation to the documents that I want to show the witness? I had thought that I had very carefully checked all the documents in the binders which related to the radio station. Needless to say, I left out two, which was discovered yesterday by a member of the team. Your Honour, I would want -- may I say the witness hasn't looked at them either, so if Your Honour allows me, he's going to be looking at them for maybe for the first time. They are -- at the moment, there are two documents, one numbered Exhibit 214, and -- P214, and the other P226, which are in the binders. We've given copies to the Defence and copies for Your Honours. And the third document was not in the binders but was disclosed. It bears the disclosure number 2.399. Your Honour, I'm perfectly well aware that I haven't given advance notice to the Defence or Your Honours of these documents. I would wish to put them in. I don't anticipate that we will reach them today because I'm going to be taking the documents in chronological order but, Your Honour, my application would be, despite the fact that no advance notice has been given, I would wish to put these documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, do I understand you well, while the first two of these documents have an exhibit number already, the third one hasn't? No?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct, all it's got at the moment is the disclosure number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take this matter first. Mr. Ackerman, do you have any major problems with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only problem I have right now, Your Honour, is that I don't have P214. I was given 226 and 2.399, but I don't have 214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. P214 is disclosure number 3.341.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I have no objection, Your Honour, to any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Maitre de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] I have no problems with these documents whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci. So we can, I suppose, bring in the witness, or do you have anything else to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we'll go into closed session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there is also one matter that the Chamber would like to raise. And also, Ms. Korner, you have tendered [redacted] but not completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought I had forgotten to do that. Can I ask that be marked Exhibit P480.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how it will be. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to return to the 90(H) matter just very briefly. I have filed my motion. The Prosecution has responded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also General Talic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I want to say to the Chamber - and if you want me to say it in writing then I need to get your permission to respond to the Prosecutor - but I've changed my view slightly. And that is that I am impressed by the proposition that it might be either difficult or impossible for a Trial Chamber to declare a rule void, and I think the more reasonable way to approach it, and what I probably should have requested in my motion, was the proposition that where there is a conflict between a rule and an article of the Statute, that the article of the Statute must prevail, and that wouldn't involve declaring any part of a rule void but simply giving preference to the Statute as controlling in that kind of a situation. If you'd like me to put that in writing, I'd be happy to do that, but that's -- if this is going to be certified to the Appeals Court, that's actually the argument I want to make when we get to that point, and I don't think it would be appropriate for me to do that without having first brought it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that you do that. At least for the record, it would be better. The other matter that -- do you want to raise any matter, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is one small thing that we have discussed and we would like to raise with you. You will recall that earlier on, I think last week it was, you had very kindly sat down and agreed amongst yourselves to indicate your preferences as far as breaks that will be required for you to reorganise yourselves between now and the end of July. We have gone through your suggestions very carefully and we agree with practically all of them. There is one reservation that we would like to make and bring to your attention. You are proposing that this Chamber does not sit on the 3rd, 4th and 5th and then on the 8th and 9th of July. In other words, it would be the 3rd through the 9th of July. What prompts us actually to deal with this is that we notice that immediately after, there are three days which will be dedicated for the Plenary, and then there is a Saturday and a Sunday, which would mean that basically we would have five plus seven, 12 days' break in the beginning of July, following basically a long weekend at the end of June when you have -- when we have the court maintenance. We were proposing -- going to propose to you that the five days, actual working days, that you had proposed as -- for a break, that is the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 8th and 9th, will be moved to the end of the month, namely 29th, 30th and 31st of July and then 1st and 2nd. What would the advantages of such a shift mean? It would mean that you would still have five days' break in the second day -- second week of July. We won't have any because we have the Plenary, but you can have five days there, and it would enable you to go home for your summer recess holidays a good week in advance than you -- what you would normally do. In other words, the summer recess starts on the 3rd of August right through the 23rd of August. This way, the summer recess, for the intents and purposes of this trial, would practically start on the 27th of July, that being a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour that particular holiday I assented to because I didn't want to upset the great American holiday. I'm not anxious to have that holiday. I didn't ask for the queen's silver whatever it is, jubilee, birthday, nor did Mr. Cayley. My anxiety is that we sit as often as possible, but Mr. Ackerman - and as I say, I didn't want to upset American sensibilities - asked for that time off. I'm very concerned about trying to get through the evidence in this case. So I'm not asking for that break. It's really Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, our suggestion is forget about 3rd, 4th, 5th, 8th, and 9th. We will work on those days. I'm sure that your patriotism, Mr. Ackerman, will not suffer because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I thought it was particularly appropriate -- I'll accept your change. I thought it was particularly appropriate this year to emphasise our separation from the British, in view of this ridiculous Rule 90(H)(ii), and give you some of the reasons why we might have done that. That would be one for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very kind of Your Honours to give us that extra week, but if that is simply to replace that earlier holiday then we wouldn't ask for it. If Your Honours don't have any particular reason for giving that break at the end of July, then I'm perfectly content to work through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As I've said, Your Honours, I'm happy with the change you've suggested, and I think it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maitre de Roux, the 14 juillet is safe because it's a Sunday this year, so you don't have to worry about that. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a Sunday. No. We agree with the proposals that you have made, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we will move those five days to the end of the month and we will leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's a month's break for the summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, basically. It's the same amount of days but instead of stopping for 12 days -- because actually, as proposed initially, there would be five days off in the first week of July, seven days off in the second week of July, and three days off in the third week of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want any of that. I mean literally, Your Honours, what I'm saying is from the point of view of the Prosecution, the -- we agreed to the suggestion made by Mr. Ackerman because it was the 4th of July, but what we are saying is there is no necessity to have these breaks and we could get on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole idea of having five, 12, 15 out of 21 days off in the first three weeks of July is a little bit -- so this way you will enjoy --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm saying the opposite. I'm saying no breaks other than the Plenary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But breaks are necessary too for everyone. We also have to liaise with our legal staff at the end of each month in particular, to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm simply making the point, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Making sure that all the summaries are in order, that the classification of bits and pieces of evidence under the various charges, we also have to do that from the very beginning. Otherwise, if we leave that to accumulate, we will never get there. Okay. At this point in time we will be able to formalise this and we will have it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, there is just one other matter which I meant to mention yesterday and I can do in one minute. I had a look at the indictment, as clearly Madam Fauveau has been doing yesterday, over the mosques in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are all 1993 ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, they are all destroyed, they are not damaged, but it appears the one mosque that everybody agrees was severely damaged isn't listed. I'm merely giving notice at this stage that I will be applying at some stage towards the end of this case to add that particular mosque to the indictment. As to what the others -- the evidence -- there is still more evidence to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let me not make any comments at this stage. Okay. So I thank you all. Thanks also to the interpreters, as usual. Without you, we would be in a big mess in here. And my apologies if sometimes we make your lives difficult. We will resume our labours tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.46 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
